## Setup

Inline maths like $\hat H \psi = E \psi$, and display maths with tags you can
reference:

$$
\left[ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2 + V(\mathbf r) \right]\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)
= \varepsilon_{n\mathbf k}\,\psi_{n\mathbf k}(\mathbf r)
$$ {#eq-ks}

Refer back to it as @eq-ks. Multi-line derivations use `aligned`:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma(\mathbf r, \mathbf r'; \omega)
  &= \frac{i}{2\pi}\int d\omega'\, G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r'; \omega+\omega')\,
     W(\mathbf r,\mathbf r'; \omega') e^{i\omega'\eta} \\
  &\approx \Sigma_x + \Sigma_c .
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.callout-tip}
## Result
Use callouts (`note`, `tip`, `warning`, `important`) to flag the thing you
will want to find again in six months.
:::

## Code and results

```{python}
#| label: fig-example
#| fig-cap: "Caption shown under the figure. Cross-reference it as @fig-example."
#| code-fold: true

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

k = np.linspace(-np.pi, np.pi, 400)
plt.plot(k, -2 * np.cos(k))
plt.xlabel(r"$k$")
plt.ylabel(r"$\varepsilon(k)$ (eV)")
plt.show()
```

Cite sources with `[@key]` if you set a `bibliography` above [@key].
